results.title: Nebius removes its spot-price ceiling — preemptible GPUs can now cost more than on-demand | GPUJournal
highlights:
Nov 2, 2026

In an update note dated Nov 2, 2026 on its own blog, Nebius says the cap that kept its dynamic spot price one cent below the on-demand rate is gone. Spot still has a floor — it just no longer has a top, and setting your own max price is now the only brake.

Image: Nebius via nebius.com

What changed, from Nebius's own post “Introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs” (published Sep 22, 2026; read Nov 2, 2026): its update note, dated Nov 2, 2026, reads — “this section previously stated that the spot price always stays between a floor and a ceiling one cent below the on-demand rate. We have removed the ceiling. Customers can cap what they pay by setting a max price.” The post's how-it-works section now states plainly: “There is no upper limit, so during periods of high demand the spot price can rise above the on-demand GPU-hour rate.”

How the mechanism works, in the same post: the spot price for a GPU type in a region is set from available capacity and real-time demand, recalculated up to every 15 minutes, and it still cannot fall below a set floor — only the ceiling has gone. A renter who sets a max price keeps the old protection by hand: when spot rises above the cap, the instance stops, data is retained, and it can restart when the price falls back — automatically for Kubernetes clusters, manually (or via Terraform, SDK, API or CLI) for standalone VMs. A renter who instead chose to follow the spot price has no cap at all after today's change.

What did not change: Nebius's on-demand list. Re-read on Nebius's own prices page on Nov 2, 2026, B300 is $9.50 an hour, B200 $8.50, H200 $5.40, H100 $4.50, RTX PRO 6000 $1.80 and L40S from $1.55 — every figure the same as our Nov 1 read. This is not a price rise in the list; it is the removal of the guarantee that the interruptible lane is always the cheaper one.

...

A spot price that can pass the on-demand rate in a busy hour inverts that pitch exactly when capacity is tightest — which, in the autumn pattern this journal has been tracking (Nebius's own across-the-board rise on Oct 1, Verda's eight rises since Oct 23, SaladCloud's ... Rising prices and now an uncapped spot market are consistent with growing demand for GPUs (our reading of the pattern, labelled as interpretation).

### What it means if you rent GPUs

If you rent preemptible VMs on Nebius, do one thing today: set a max price. The ceiling that used to do that job for you was removed on Nov 2, and a workload set to follow the spot price can now be billed above the on-demand rate in a high-demand hour — paying a premium for capacity that can still be reclaimed. The discount lane still exists, but from today the discount is something you enforce yourself.

results.author: Kristijan Sekereš
highlights:
Nebius list prices in US dollars, the only billing currency outside Israel, VAT excluded, checked 15 and 16 October 2026.

...

### GPUs

GPU VMs are billed per second. On the H100, H200, B200, B300 and RTX PRO 6000 the GPU-hour price includes the preset's vCPUs and RAM (16 vCPUs and 200 GB per H100); disks are extra.

| GPU | Regions | USD per GPU-hour | EUR | Default quota |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 80 GB | eu-north1 (Finland) only | 4.50 | 4.01 | 32 |
| H200 141 GB | eu-north1, eu-west1 (France), us-central1 | 5.40 | 4.82 | 32 in Finland, 8 in France, 0 in us-central1 |
| B200 | us-central1, me-west1 (Israel) | 8.50 | 7.58 | 0 |
| B300 | eu-west2 (France), uk-south1, us-north1 | 9.50 | 8.48 | 32 in each |
| RTX PRO 6000 96 GB | eu-south1 (Madrid), uk-south2, us-central1 | 1.80 | 1.61 | 32, except 0 in us-central1 |
| L40S 48 GB | eu-north1 | from 1.55 | 1.38 | 32 |
| GB200, GB300 NVL72 | not listed per region | "Contact us" | | sales |

...

Preemptible and committed. Since 8 October 2026 spot prices move: "from" USD 0.99 per GPU-hour on B300 and B200 and USD 0.79 on H200, H100 and RTX PRO 6000, changing "as often as every 15 minutes", up to "one cent below the current pay-as-you-go (PAYG) on-demand rate". Commitments promise "up to 35% less than on-demand rates" for multi-month cluster reservations, for companies only, through sales, with no public price list. Rack-scale systems are sold that way too, and their fee covers the whole rack, including a "Maintenance Buffer" of 2 of its 18 nodes.

Price changes. On-demand GPU prices rose on 1 June and again on 1 October 2026, in USD per GPU-hour:

| GPU | Until 31 May 2026 | From 1 June | From 1 October | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | 2.95 | 3.85 | 4.50 | +52.5% |
| H200 | 3.50 | 4.50 | 5.40 | +54.3% |
| B200 | 5.50 | 7.15 | 8.50 | +54.5% |
| B300 | 6.10 | 7.85 | 9.50 | +55.7% |

The October step is in the current pricing documentation; the earlier prices come from archived copies of Nebius's pages. On 1 October CPU-only VMs rose too: the Genoa vCPU by 25% and RAM by 41%. An archived copy of the documentation still showed the H100 at 3.85 with no notice on 26 September 2026; the copy of 29 September announced the change. The contract requires notice "at least three (3) calendar days prior to any increase in Service Rates"; we found no record of earlier notice.

results.title: Nebius vs AWS - Software Spotlight
highlights:
| Criterion | Nebius | AWS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positioning | AI cloud: GPU clusters plus training and inference platform | General cloud with a large GPU and ML catalog |
| GPU models listed (aggregator count) | 8 | 18 |
| H100 on-demand per GPU-hour | $4.50 | $6.88 |
| H200 on-demand per GPU-hour | $5.40 | $7.91 |
| B200 on-demand per GPU-hour | $8.50 | $14.24 |
| B300 on-demand per GPU-hour | $9.50 | $17.80 |
| Billing options | On-demand, preemptible/spot | On-demand, reserved (12 or 36 months) |
| Egress to internet | Free from VMs; Object Storage egress billed | 100 GB/month free, then $0.09 per GB (North America) |
| Locations | 10 | 36 |
| Managed Slurm | Yes (Soperator), size limits on managed tier | Available through separate AWS offerings |
| Managed Kubernetes | Yes | Yes |
| Founded, headquarters | 2022, Netherlands | 2006, USA |

Prices come from a getdeploying comparison with both datasets updated November 4, 2026, cross-checked against the Nebius documentation for Nebius figures. They are list prices before taxes, regions and discounts. Verify against the AWS EC2 pricing page before you commit.

...

On the November 4, 2026 snapshot, Nebius was lower on every NVIDIA model both providers list. The H100 gap was $2.38 per GPU-hour, or about 35% below AWS. An eight-GPU H100 node running continuously for a 30-day month (720 hours) works out to roughly $25,900 on Nebius at $4.50 per GPU-hour versus about $39,600 on AWS at $6.88. The calculation is arithmetic on list prices and ignores storage, networking, support plans and any enterprise discount.

Three caveats matter more than the headline gap:

1. Reserved and committed pricing. AWS lists reserved terms of 12 or 36 months. The aggregator shows GB200 at $10.58 reserved on AWS, where Nebius shows “on request.” Large AWS customers often negotiate private pricing that public lists do not show.
2. Nebius price movement. A third-party tracker reports Nebius raised on-demand H100, H200, B200 and B300 rates effective October 1, 2026. Older comparisons showing lower Nebius prices are stale.
3. Preemptible capacity. Nebius lists preemptible GPUs from $0.79 to $0.99 per GPU-hour. These are interruptible and the price floats, so they suit checkpointed jobs, not deadline-bound runs.

results.title: What a million tokens costs on a rented H100 or B200 — Die Brief
results.author: The Die Brief Desk
highlights:
Nebius posts 4.50 dollars an hour for an H100 and 8.50 for a B200 from 8 October 2026. Lambda posts 3.99 and 6.69 on its instance page. Neither page prices a million tokens.

...

Nebius prints the rates in its document Compute pricing in Nebius AI Cloud. The page says on-demand prices for B300, B200, H200, and H100 changed on 1 October 2026, and that from 8 October 2026 the preemptible price on several of those platforms is a dynamic spot rate, displayed as a floor. The dollar figures on that page are before tax. The billing unit is one second and the pricing unit is one hour, so thirty minutes is half the hourly rate. A stopped virtual machine is not charged for the GPU. The bars are the on-demand rates read on 10 October 2026. The 8 October note on that page is a preemptible floor, and it is not drawn. The line above the bars is what an H100 hour has cost across the months a posted rate could be read.

NVIDIA B300 NVLink is 9.50 dollars for one GPU-hour, with a preemptible floor of 0.99 dollars. Before 1 October the same block lists 7.85 dollars on demand. NVIDIA B200 NVLink is 8.50 dollars for one GPU-hour. The page ties one platform id to us-central1 and another to me-west1, at the same on-demand rate, with a preemptible floor of 0.99 dollars. Before 1 October that block lists 7.15 dollars. NVIDIA H200 NVLink is 5.40 dollars, in eu-north1, eu-north2, eu-west1, and us-central1, with a preemptible floor of 0.79 dollars. Before 1 October it lists 4.50 dollars. NVIDIA H100 NVLink is 4.50 dollars, and the page says that platform is only in eu-north1. The preemptible floor is 0.79 dollars. Before 1 October it lists 3.85 dollars.

NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 stays at 1.80 dollars a GPU-hour across the October change, with a preemptible floor of 0.79 dollars from 8 October. NVIDIA L40S is listed as 1.35 dollars for the GPU plus separate CPU and memory lines. Because the page does not roll those into one GPU-hour, this brief does not invent an all-in rate. The page does not list a public hourly price for a Rubin rack or a GB200 NVL72, so those rows stay blank, and it does not print tokens per second beside any GPU.

Lambda's instance page, opened the same day, lists the chip, the onboard memory, the vCPUs, and a price per GPU-hour, plus applicable tax. The B200 SXM6 row with 180 GB and 208 vCPUs is 6.69 dollars. The H100 SXM row with 80 GB and 208 vCPUs is 3.99 dollars. The A100 SXM row with 80 GB and 240 vCPUs is 2.79 dollars. The page groups further rows under smaller instance sizes. B200 SXM6 appears again at 6.79, 6.89, and 6.99 dollars, next to 104, 52, and 26 vCPUs.

...

An H100 hour has not moved in one smooth line, and the two rates on the chart are different offers. The SXM5 pay-as-you-go hour was $4.85 from November 2023 through July 2024, and $3.50 on 15 September 2024. The later NVLink hour was $2.95 from October 2025 through May 2026, $3.85 from 1 June 2026, and $4.50 from 1 October 2026. The months between September 2024 and November 2025 are left empty. The posted offer changed, and those in-between months were not in the copies read for this brief. A third quote, $2.118 for the GPU alone with the processor and memory billed beside it, is not drawn.

The useful update is the dated move on the Nebius page itself. From 1 October 2026 the on-demand H100 line goes from 3.85 to 4.50 dollars, the H200 line from 4.50 to 5.40, the B200 line from 7.15 to 8.50, and the B300 line from 7.85 to 9.50. Those four pairs are on one document, with the old rate left in place under a "before" heading. Lambda's instance rows do not carry a date. The 6.69 and 3.99 dollar figures are what that URL showed on 10 October 2026, and a revision should open the URL again rather than treat them as a contract.

results.title: Nebius Raises On-Demand GPU Prices Up to 21% From October 1: What an H100 Hour Now Costs | ServerCalc
results.author: ServerCalc Editorial
highlights:
From October 1, 2026, Nebius raised its on-demand, pay-as-you-go rates across its four current Nvidia platforms. On its own published price list the per-GPU-hour numbers now read: H100 NVLink at $4.50, up from $3.85 (about 17%); H200 NVLink at $5.40, up from $4.50 (20%); B200 NVLink at $8.50, up from $7.15 (about 19%); and B300 NVLink at $9.50, up from $7.85 (21%). CPU-only servers were caught in the same round — the AMD EPYC Genoa vCPU now lists at $0.015 per CPU-hour, roughly a quarter more than before. Separately, from October 8 the provider moved preemptible capacity for these platforms onto dynamic spot pricing, so the cheap interruptible tier no longer has a fixed rate.

These are list prices for on-demand use. Committed and reserved terms are quoted separately and run well below the hourly rate; the increase lands hardest on buyers who pay by the hour with no commitment.
